name: Xylitol gum

lead: Xylitol gum is chewing gum sweetened with a sugar alcohol instead of sugar. Users chew it to cut down plaque bacteria and get more saliva.
Several randomized trials measured mutans streptococci and plaque, and a 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found reduced plaque. Cochrane found the evidence for most xylitol products insufficient.

paras: Xylitol is thought to suppress growth of pathogenic oral streptococci, and chewing stimulates saliva.
High intake can cause gas and diarrhea. Xylitol is toxic to dogs, and the FDA considers it safe as a sweetener for people.

lead: Xylitol gum is chewing gum sweetened with xylitol, a sugar alcohol, rather than sugar. It is promoted for reducing cavity-causing bacteria and plaque and for stimulating saliva.[1][2]

Trials have measured mutans streptococci in plaque and saliva after xylitol gum, including a dose-response study of 132 participants.[1] A 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found that xylitol chewing gum reduces plaque, while a 2015 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for most xylitol products other than fluoride toothpaste.[2]
infobox: Laxative effect at high intake; toxic to dogs

paras: Xylitol is thought to suppress growth of pathogenic oral streptococci.[2] In a randomized dose-response trial, participants chewed gum providing 0 (control), 3.44, 6.88 or 10.32 g of xylitol daily and had mutans streptococci measured at baseline, 5 weeks and 6 months.[1] Another trial in young adults compared xylitol gum, probiotic gum, a combination and placebo gum over several weeks.[3] Earlier work includes a 24-month school-based caries study and a 1984 study of plaque and saliva S. mutans levels.[4][5]
A trial in day-care children also tested xylitol gum for preventing acute otitis media.[6]

High intakes of xylitol can cause gas, diarrhea and IBS-like symptoms.[2] Xylitol is toxic to dogs, with insulin release and hypoglycemia reported at around 100 mg/kg and liver failure likely above 500 mg/kg.[2] The US FDA considers xylitol safe as a sugar substitute.[2]

Human trials include the 132-person dose-response study of mutans streptococci,[1] a randomized study in 80 young adults comparing xylitol and probiotic gums,[3] a 24-month school-based caries trial,[4] a 1984 trial on plaque and saliva S. mutans,[5] and a 857-child trial of xylitol products for otitis media.[6] Reviews of sugar substitutes and chewing gum for caries have also been published.[7] Wikipedia notes that evidence for xylitol products other than fluoride toothpaste is considered insufficient by the Cochrane review.[2]
